title: Culture-Fair Test Challenge
summary: Students design a non-verbal reasoning task through six decisions and watch six construct-irrelevant demands respond. Removing language removes one of them. Four fictional participants, described only by prior experience of testing formats, show how unevenly a design distributes demands that have nothing to do with reasoning.
learningObjectives: Explain why removing language from a test removes the reading demand and leaves the others intact.
Distinguish construct-relevant from construct-irrelevant demands, and use that framing instead of 'culture-free'.
Explain opportunity to learn a test format as a fact about exposure rather than about capacity.
State what evidence is required before scores from different groups can be treated as comparable.
Recognise that reducing construct-irrelevant demand costs administration time, and is a design decision rather than a discovered property.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout; each design option carries its consequence as text beneath the label. The demand chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table rating each demand 'high', 'moderate' or 'low' in words. The construct-share bar prints its own labels and percentages inside each segment and repeats them in the note beneath, so the split never depends on the fill colours. Participant cards state the load as text as well as showing a meter. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Culture-fair testing: construct-irrelevant demand, opportunity to learn a format, and what comparability requires
simulationNotes: A design model with illustrative values written for this tool; no published test is described. Six construct-irrelevant demands are tracked, combined by maximum rather than sum, and converted to a construct-relevant share by a simple linear rule. The four fictional participants are characterised ONLY by prior experience of testing formats, devices and puzzle conventions: no nationality, ethnicity, region, language or group membership appears anywhere in the tool, and no group difference of any kind is simulated. The tool produces no score, ability estimate or performance prediction for any person, fictional or real; the participant figure is a count of demands the design makes that the person has not had opportunity to become familiar with, and the page states this explicitly wherever it appears.
